Kulārṇava Tantra
------------------------------------------
The Kulārṇava Tantra is an important work of the कौल school. (See TANTRAS.) As per the colophon given at the end of each chapter (called as ‘ullāsa’ here) it is a part of a much bigger work, the Ūrdhvāmnyāya Tantra, comprising 1,25,000 verses. However, this work has not so for been discovered. For all practical purposes this can be considered as an independent work having 2060 verses spread over 17 ullāsas or chapters.
The speciality of this work is that it offers a symbolic and spiritual interpretation of some वामाचार practices like the five ‘ma-kāras’. (See under TANTRAS.)
A brief summary or synopsis of the contents may now be attempted here:
First Ullāsa (Jīvasthitikathanam—121 Verses)
In this section there is a detailed analysis of the state of the jīvātman or the individual सोउल्.
Human birth is the greatest. One who does not seek लिबेरतिओन् even after getting this birth is an ātmaghātaka (self-killer).
Body being the instrument of sādhana, should be protected by all means.
It is tattvajñāna (knowledge of the Reality) that gives लिबेरतिओन्. Hence one should try to get it by taking refuge in a गुरु or spiritual teacher.
Second Ullāsa(Kulamāhātmyakathanam—142 verses)
‘Kula’ means the देवी or the Divine मोथेर्. Hence Kuladharma is the art and science of upāsanā (meditation and worship) on the देवी. This section deals mainly with Kuladharma.
The six darśanas (systems of philo-sophy) are actually parts of this कुल-धर्म.
How the पञ्चमकारस् have been misused by the ignorant and evil persons is described here.
Third Ullāsa (Śrīprāsāda-parāmantra- kathanam—117 verses)
This chapter deals with the paraprasādamantra, viz., ‘haṁsaḥ’ which is the great cosmic breath.
The method of पुरश्चरण (repetition of a मन्त्र in a ceremonial way) of the haṁsamantra is also described.
Fourth Ullāsa (Mahāṣoḍhānyāsakathanam—130 verses)
Ṣoḍhānyāsa or Ṣoḍānyāsa means six ways of touching the various parts of the body in ritualistic practices. It is described here in great detail.
The following six nyāsas are of great importance: Prapañcanyāsa (nyāsa involving various parts of this world like islands, oceans and mountains as related to 16 aspects of the goddess लक्ष्मी); Bhuvananyāsa (nyāsa involving the 14 lokas or worlds like अतल, वितल and associated with the goddesses at the centres or चक्रस् like मूलाधार, स्वाधिष्ठान and so on); Mūrtinyāsa (nyāsa involving 16 aspects of विष्णु like Keśava and नारायण, and associated with 16 śaktis or goddesses of letters like a, ā, i, ī, and so on, called Akṣaraśakti, Ādyā, इष्टका etc.); Mantranyāsa (nyāsa involving all the letters of the alphabet from a to kṣa, and associated with the sixteen goddesses like Eka-kūṭa-īśvarī, each of them being considered as the presiding deity of the mantras); Daivatānyāsa (nyāsa involving goddesses like निवृत्ति-अम्बा, pratiṣṭhā-अम्बा and so on, the parts of the body touched being the right toe, going round all the parts on the right side, changing over to the left and ending with the left toe); मातृकान्यास (nyāsa involving the mātṛkās or letters of the alphabet [with anusvāra] arranged in a particular order and associated with a शक्ति and her भैरव).
Fifth Ullāsa (Kulamāhātmyakathanam—114 verses)
While extolling the greatness of the Kaulamārga, it also gives many details such as the vessels needed in the rituals, various types of wine, meat, fish and other items.
An important point to be noticed is the esoteric interpretation of the five “ma”-kāras and the severe condemnation of observing them in the gross physical sense.
Sixth Ullāsa (Dravyasaṁskāravidhānam—102 verses)
It describes the characteristics of the worshipper, of the suitable place, pañcaśuddhi or five types of purification, drawing of the मण्डल (sacred diagram), vessels needed for worship, various kalās, inviting the देवी (goddess) and worshipping her, मन्त्र and यन्त्र of the goddess and meditation on the gurus (teachers) of the tradition.
Seventh Ullāsa (Baṭukaśaktyādipūjāvidhānam—104 verses)
Offering a बलि to the deity Baṭuka—described as Devīputra or son of the देवी, the Divine Mother—is stated first, with a long मन्त्र.
Then is described the ārati (waving of light) with a specially prepared lamp called ‘Kuladīpa’.
The names of eight Kulaśaktis and of eight Akulaśaktis are also given.
A long मन्त्र of 73 letters to be used at the end of the पूजा of the देवी is also described.
Some rules connected with the ceremonial drinking of madya or wine are stated towards the end.
Eighth Ullāsa (Tattvatritayapānādibheda- kathanam—111 verses)
This section deals with the चक्र or various forms of seating as also several kinds of ullāsas or bliss.
Ninth Ullāsa (Yogasaṁsthāpana- kathanam—134 verses)
This chapter deals with various aspects of योग like the characteristics of a योगि, nature of समाधि and जीवन्मुक्ति (liberation while still living) as also ब्रह्मज्ञान (knowledge of ब्रह्मन्).
The text declares that there is no difference between the जीव and परमात्मन्.
It also describes the four states of a sādhaka (novice), the need to observe the varṇāśrama dharmas, कर्मयोग and other related subjects.
Tenth Ullāsa (Viśeṣadivasārcanavidhāna—114 verses)
As the little indicates, this ullāsa is dedicated to arcana or पूजा (worship) of various kinds.
The worship is to be offered on special days like the birthdays of the गुरु, of great men, auspicious days like the eighth, fourteenth and the fifteenth days of the dark fortnight and so on.
Daily worship of the deity is considered the best.
All worship has to be planned and performed according to one’s resources, faith and suitability of time.
There are also simple descriptions of the worship of nine kumārīs (girls before puberty), nine yuvatīs (young women) and nine couples (viz., गौरी-शिव, Ramā- विष्णु, Vāṇī-ब्रह्मा, शची-इन्द्र and so on).
Mention is also made of the worship of the योगिनीस् (See YOGINĪS.) for getting relief from diseases, difficulties in life and offsetting the evil effects from bad persons.

Kullūkabhaṭṭa
------------------------------------------
The life of an average Hindu was generally guided—both at the individual and at the social level—by the smṛtis and the धर्मशास्त्रस्. Among all the smṛtis, the most ancient and the most widely accepted one is the Manusmṛti (100 B. C.).
Of all the commentaries on this work, the Manvarthamuktāvalī of कुल्लूकभट्ट is the most widely known and has been printed several times.
Kullūkabhaṭṭa was the son of भट्ट-divākara and belonged to the Vārendra family of Bengal. He must have flourished sometime during the period A. D. 1150-1300. This work was probably composed around A. D. 1250 in काशी.
His commentary is concise, lucid and to the point. He avoids all unnecessary discussions though he is quite critical of मेधातिथि (circa A. D. 825-900) and Govindarāja (11th century A. D.) both of whom also wrote commentaries on the स्मृति of मनु.
Śrāddhasāgara is another work attributed to him wherein he deals with the following topics: times and places suitable for śrāddha; aṣṭakāśrāddha which even the शूद्रस् can perform; details regarding inter-calary months; the यज्ञोपवीत or the sacred thread and so on.
This work was perhaps, a part of a bigger work called Smṛtisāgara not available now. Vivādasāgara and Aśaucasāgara are two more works, alluded to, by him, which too must have been a part of this bigger work.
Kullūkabhaṭṭa was an adept in the पूर्वमीमाṁसा doctrines.
See also MANUSMṚTI.

kulapati
(‘head of a गुरुकुल’)
------------------------------------------
Education in the olden days was completely residential. The होउसे of the आचार्य or the teacher where the students resided and learnt, was called ‘ācāryakula’.
When the campus grew big and the number of resident-students went beyond ten thousand, the chief आचार्य who was the head of the institution came to be known as ‘kulapati’.
See also GURUKULA.

Kulaparvata
(‘a mountain that demarcates’)
------------------------------------------
Purāṇic geography of the world mentions seven dvīpas (island continents) each of which (except the last) has seven Kulaparvatas. These Kulaparvatas are mountains that demarcate the lands in the above mentioned island-continents.
Bhāratavarṣa (the Indian Subcontinent) is a part of the जम्बूद्वीप. Its Kulaparvatas are: महेन्द्र, Malaya, Sahya, Śaktimān, Ṛkṣa, विन्ध्य and Pāriyātra.
Similarly there are Kulaparvatas in other dvīpas also. For instance, Gomoda in Plakṣadvīpa; Kumuda in Śālmali; Vidruma in Kuśadvīpa; वामन in Krauñcadvīpa; Raivataka in Śākadvīpa and Mānasottara in Puṣkaradvīpa.

kula
------------------------------------------
Though the literal meaning of the word is ‘clan’ or ‘family’, it has been used in a more technical sense in the tāntrik literature. ‘Kula’ is interpreted as ‘Śakti’ or the ‘Divine मोथेर्’ and the disciplines of the तन्त्रस् advocating her worship are known as ‘Kaulamārga’ or ‘Kaulācāra’. As per this definition, कुल can also mean the spiritual lineage from the गुरु to the disciple, the Ādiguru or Primeval Teacher being शिव Himself.
Kula, vaṁśa or गोत्र (lineage) is a very important factor considered especially in the settling of marriages.
